segments: The seventeenth cycle.
The Arab Kings.
[When] the small force that he had with him was confirmed,
Michael made preparations quickly and went and encamped against it.
And he too seduced certain men from the inhabitants of the city;
and one night they opened for him an old gate,
which had not been opened since the time of Constantine the Victorious.
And the Greeks entered and put it to the sword;
and Baldwin was barely able to save himself and his household,
as they embarked on a small boat and fled to Frankland.
And thus Constantinople remained once again to the Greeks,
after it had been with the Franks for a period of fifty-three years.
Now Nicephorus, the unlawful patriarch, did not live long,
but died quickly.
And King Michael set up in his place Romanus, the metropolitan {OCR: patriarch?} of the city of Adrianople.
And this man, as soon as he was appointed,
was caught in a blameworthy affair and was deposed.
Then King Michael sent and brought the Patriarch Arsenius from exile,
and promised him that he would release Kaloyan, the king's son, from prison,
and hand over to him his father's kingdom,
while he himself
would hold Constantinople
alone,
which he had taken by the sword.
And the Patriarch prayed over him,
and was reconciled,
and sat again upon the throne.
Now that Michael, when he had appeased the Patriarch,
added evil upon evil,
and instead of releasing Kaloyan from prison and making him king,
he sent and gouged out his pupils and blinded his eyes.
Now when the Patriarch understood this,
he deposed himself again
and returned to his confinement.
And the king brought an archimandrite whose name was Joseph and made him patriarch,
and behold, he stands at the head today.
And in those very days of winter,
while these evils were being accomplished in Melitene,
Hulagu, the king of kings, went down against Baghdad,
and Baiju also arrived from the land of the Romans.
And the forces of the Baghdadis went outside to encounter the Tatars.
And those who were standing at their head were:
the great Kurdish emir, who was called Bar Kurar,
and the lesser Dawitdar, the servant of the Caliph.
